newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: FORECAST - Yugo 1996 GDP to rise 5-6 pct - ministry.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Yugo 1996 GDP to rise 5-6 pct - ministry.

text.p: Yugoslavia's 1996 gross domestic product (GDP) is likely to rise five or six percent, almost retaining its 1995 growth rate, the government's Centre for Development and Economics said on Friday.

"It is clear that earlier forecasts of 12.5 percent GDP rise will not be achieved and this year's growth would range between five and six percent," director of the centre Misa Jandric told a news conference.
According to government figures, Yugoslavia's GDP grew six percent in 1995 to $15.91 billion from $14.974 billion the previous year.
The 1995 figure was 44.7 percent below the 1990 level, according to the study presented at the news conference.
The data was calculated with new methodology recognized by the United Nations, based on the system of national accounts.

"Implementing the new system to calculate key macroeconomic indicators, Yugoslavia met demands of international financial institutions to present reliable information on the social and economic state of the country," Zivkovic said.
The new system of calculating GDP includes the services sector -- education, culture, health system, banking, insurance, state and defence.
Head of the Federal Statistics Office Milovan Zivkovic said the figures showed per capita income reached $1,510 in 1995 -- almost half the 1990 figure.
"Despite all difficulties and U.N. sanctions in past five years, only Slovenia and the Czech Republic are ahead of Yugoslavia in terms of per capita income (in Eastern Europe)," Zivkovic said.
Yugoslav minister for development, science and environment Janko Radulovic said the country would need at least six to seven years to reach its pre-1990 level.
The government's centre has calculated that GDP grew 2.3 percent during first eight months of 1996.
Industrial output rose 1.3 percent and agriculture 0.8 percent over the 1995 average. Transportation activities surged 12.7 percent while trade jumped by 5.5 percent.
At the same time, catering and tourism fell 4.1 percent and construction by 11.4 percent, the study said.

"The slowdown in overall economic activity mainly resulted from unfavourable trade balance and rising trade deficit. Lack of working capital was another hinderance," the study said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
